source.title: Bilateral Ground Reaction Force Asymmetry During Supramaximal Drop Landings

paper.citation: Barker, L., & Harry, J. (2022). Bilateral ground reaction force asymmetry during supramaximal drop landings. International Journal of Strength and Conditioning, 2(1). https://doi.org/10.47206/ijsc.v2i1.160
paper.abstract: How do impact and attenuation impulses and bilateral vertical-ground-reaction-force asymmetries change as healthy adults land from progressively higher, including supramaximal, drop heights? Nineteen healthy, recreationally active college students completed the protocol: 14 men and five women, mean age 21.3 years, with 4.4 years of weight-training experience. Participants could back squat at least 1.25 times body mass; average relative one-repetition maximum was 1.72. No participants were injured or undergoing return-to-sport rehabilitation. Secondary analysis of pre-existing data from bilateral drop landings progressing from 0.30 to 1.52 m in 0.15-m increments. Force-platform outcomes included peak vertical force, loading rate, impact impulse, attenuation impulse, total impulse, and bilateral asymmetry ratios. Group and individual linear regressions related each outcome to drop height; significance was set at .05.
paper.tldr: This exploratory analysis shows that bilateral force asymmetry can change with task intensity, challenging interpretation of a single low-intensity landing test. All group asymmetry slopes were negative as height increased, but adjusted R² values were only .06–.15, so drop height explained little group-level asymmetry variance. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Secondary analysis of pre-existing data from bilateral drop landings progressing from 0.30 to 1.52 m in 0.15-m increments. Force-platform outcomes included peak vertical force, loading rate, impact impulse, attenuation impulse, total impulse, and bilateral asymmetry ratios. Group and individual linear regressions related each outcome to drop height; significance was set at .05.
paper.findings: All group asymmetry slopes were negative as height increased, but adjusted R² values were only .06–.15, so drop height explained little group-level asymmetry variance. Individual responses varied: seven participants showed height-related attenuation-impulse asymmetry patterns with adjusted R² values of .23–.64, while impact-impulse patterns were notable in nine participants. Impact impulse remained approximately 19% of attenuation impulse across heights at the group level (adjusted R²=.0001 for change in the ratio). The study did not test whether any asymmetry measure predicted injury, reinjury, readiness, or successful return to sport.
paper.limitations: Small healthy convenience sample, mixed sex, and no injured or competitive-athlete comparison limit transfer to rehabilitation. Repeated trials across extreme heights may involve learning, fatigue, apprehension, and strategy changes not isolated by the analysis. Multiple individual regressions in 19 participants increase false-positive risk; no multiplicity control or independent replication is described. Reduced asymmetry at a higher task demand is not necessarily safer or more normal; it may simply constrain movement options. The highest drop was 4.34 times average CMJ height and exceeds typical team-sport landing demands. No chronic training study has shown that supramaximal drops improve eccentric performance or prevent injury.
paper.practicalImplications: Task intensity is a measurement condition, not a treatment. Standardize and document drop height relative to athlete capacity before comparing asymmetry over time. Do not add extreme drops solely to obtain a more symmetrical score, and do not use this study to justify return-to-play clearance. Any high-drop assessment requires appropriate clinical oversight, progressive exposure, competence, and a sport-specific rationale.

paper.rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, task intensity is a measurement condition, not a treatment.
